messages.content: On what dates did The Family of Man open and close at the Museum of Modern Art in New York?
The Family of Man was on view at the Museum of Modern Art, New York, from January 24 to May 8, 1955.
Who curated The Family of Man, and who served as the curatorial assistant?
The Family of Man was curated by Edward Steichen, then Director of the Department of Photography at the Museum of Modern Art, assisted by Wayne Miller.
Who designed the installation of The Family of Man at MoMA in 1955?
The installation was designed by the architect Paul Rudolph, who used temporary walls and varied print sizes ranging from 24 x 36 cm to 300 x 400 cm.
How many photographs, photographers, and countries are conventionally cited for The Family of Man?
The conventional figures, carried by both MoMA's archives-highlights page and the UNESCO Memory of the World register, are 503 photographs by 273 photographers from 68 countries.
Who wrote the prologue for The Family of Man, and what was its connection to Steichen?

The prologue was written by Carl Sandburg, Steichen's brother-in-law. The exhibition's title comes from Sandburg's 1944 poem 'The Long Shadow of Lincoln: A Litany.' The prologue was distributed to visitors as a leaflet and reprinted in full in both editions of the catalog.
Which W. Eugene Smith photograph is recorded as the closing image of The Family of Man?
The closing image, per MoMA's archives-highlights page, is W. Eugene Smith's A Walk to Paradise Garden (1946), recorded as photo-0488 in this repository.
What is the highest plate number printed in the MoMA Master Checklist for The Family of Man, and how many out-of-range three-digit plates exist?
The main numerical sequence runs to plate #503. There are also two out-of-range three-digit plates, #505 and #506, plus one letter-suffix sub-plate (#404A), per the MoMA Master Checklist.
Who designed the layout of the 1955 catalog of The Family of Man?

The catalog layout was designed by Leo Lionni, who is described in the MoMA press release of June 21, 1955 as a 'well-known art director and artist.' The catalog was printed by R.R. Donnelley and Sons.
Who published the deluxe edition of the 1955 The Family of Man catalog, and what was its page count and price?

The deluxe edition was published by Simon and Schuster in collaboration with Maco Magazine Corporation for the Museum of Modern Art. It was 226 pages and sold for $10. A separate paper edition (192 pages) was published by Maco Magazine Corporation for MoMA at $1.
Who photographed plate #4 of the Prologue (the Belgian Congo image)?
Plate #4 of the Prologue, set in the Belgian Congo, is credited in the MoMA Master Checklist to Nat Farbman (LIFE), with nationality given as American.
How many plates by Wayne Miller appear in The Family of Man, and what is notable about his earliest plates in the checklist?

Wayne Miller is represented by twelve plates (count verified by strict-match grep against the catalog data). Six of these appear within the first 47 checklist numbers (#22, #29, #42, #43, #44, #47), making him the most represented contributor in that range, and three of those (#42-#44) are concentrated in the Childbirth section.
Where and when was Edward Steichen born?

Edward Steichen (Edouard Jean Steichen) was born on 27 March 1879 in Bivange, Luxembourg. According to the CNA's biographical page, he was barely two years old when his parents emigrated to the United States.
During which years was Edward Steichen director of the Department of Photography at the Museum of Modern Art?
Edward Steichen served as Director of the Department of Photography at the Museum of Modern Art in New York from 1947 to 1962, per the CNA Luxembourg educational portal.
How many plates does Henri Cartier-Bresson have in The Family of Man, and through which agency are they credited?
Henri Cartier-Bresson is represented by eleven plates in The Family of Man (count verified against data/photographs.csv). All are credited via Magnum in the MoMA Master Checklist.
When was Magnum Photos founded, and who were its co-founders?
Magnum Photos was founded in 1947 by Henri Cartier-Bresson, Robert Capa, David 'Chim' Seymour, George Rodger, and William Vandivert. The standard scholarly roster lists those five as the co-founders.
When and where did Robert Capa die, and what assignment was he on?

Robert Capa was killed by a land mine on 25 May 1954 near Thai-Binh in Indochina, while on assignment for LIFE magazine covering the final weeks of the First Indochina War. He died nine months before The Family of Man opened, so his contribution to the exhibition is posthumous.
How many plates does Dorothea Lange have in The Family of Man, and what proportion are explicitly credited to her FSA period?

Dorothea Lange is represented by nine plates in The Family of Man (count verified by strict-match grep against data/photographs.csv on 2026-05-07). Three of the nine carry an explicit Farm Security Administration commissioner credit (photo-0093, photo-0376, photo-0379), placing them in her 1935-1939 federal documentary work.
Which Ansel Adams photograph is conventionally identified as his contribution to The Family of Man, and where was it positioned?

Adams's single plate in The Family of Man is conventionally identified as Mount Williamson, recorded as photo-0258 in this repository's data and described in secondary sources as the floor-to-ceiling backdrop to the Section 25 'Relationships' grouping. The MoMA Master Checklist records the print at 140 x 168 cm, while Wikipedia describes the installed image at 10 x 12 feet -- a dimensional discrepancy that may reflect a separately-fabricated installation print versus a smaller print held on file. The source attribution is contested at this level of detail.
What nationality does the MoMA Master Checklist record for Robert Frank, and how many of his plates appear?

The MoMA Master Checklist credits all seven of Robert Frank's plates as 'Swiss,' since Frank had not yet naturalized as a U.S. citizen at the time of the 1955 opening. His seven plates span photographs taken in the USA, Spain, Peru, Wales, and England, drawn from his early-1950s freelance period.
Where in The Family of Man do Robert Doisneau's three plates appear?

Three of Robert Doisneau's plates -- checklist numbers #14, #16, and #20 -- are clustered in Section 2 'Lovers,' all set in France, all credited via the Rapho Guillumette agency. Two further Doisneau plates appear later in the exhibition (photo-0225, photo-0238 in this repository's data, both in the 'relationships and community' cluster); the photographer-bio research note focuses on the Section-2 cluster.
In what year was Dorothea Lange awarded the first Guggenheim Fellowship given to a woman?
Dorothea Lange received the first Guggenheim Fellowship awarded to a woman in 1941, per the ICP archive page.
What were the six U.S. cities, beyond New York, on the 1955-1956 domestic tour of The Family of Man?

The six U.S. domestic-tour stops, listed in MoMA's June 21, 1955 press release, were: Minneapolis (Minneapolis Institute of Art), Dallas (Dallas Museum of Fine Arts), Cleveland (Cleveland Museum of Art), Philadelphia (Philadelphia Museum of Art), Baltimore (Baltimore Museum of Art), and Pittsburgh (Carnegie Institute). A separate international edition opened at the Corcoran Gallery in Washington, D.C., from June 30 to July 31, 1955.
Which U.S. government agency commissioned the international touring versions of The Family of Man?

The international tour was commissioned by the United States Information Agency (USIA), per the CNA Luxembourg educational portal, which describes the USIA as a Cold War-era American governmental unit created to promote a positive image of the United States.
What logistical figures does the CNA give for each touring copy of The Family of Man?

Per the CNA's educational portal, ten copies of the exhibition (with minor changes) were sent to nearly 160 towns. Each copy weighed one and a half tonnes, was packed in twenty-three crates, and required more than six days to be mounted and installed.
What different end-dates do CNA institutional sources give for the world tour of The Family of Man?

Three CNA-published institutional pages give three different end-dates: the English-language collections page gives 1962, the educational portal gives 1964 (matching the Luxembourg donation arrival), and the Steichen biography page gives 1965. The discrepancy is plausible because the multi-copy circulation could yield different last-public-showing, last-institutional-venue, and Steichen-career-end dates -- but no single end-date can be defended from the institutional sources alone. Sandeen and Turner have both engaged the multi-copy circulation question.
Which venue hosted The Family of Man in West Berlin in 1955, and how is the venue claim anchored?

The West Berlin venue was the Hochschule fur Bildende Kunste (today Universitat der Kunste Berlin). The venue claim is anchored to a NARA RG 306 photo caption (photo no. 306-FM-3) reproduced verbatim in the C2DH article 'Following The Family of Man World Tour' (2025), which documents the Berlin stop in 1955 and notes Bertolt Brecht's border crossing from East Berlin to visit the show.
Where and when was The Family of Man shown in Johannesburg, and which version of the country's name does the CNA use?

Per the CNA educational portal, the show was on view at the Government Pavilion in Johannesburg from August 30 to September 13, 1958, in what the caption labels the Union of South Africa. The CNA's wider sample list also names 'Zimbabwe,' an anachronism since the country was Southern Rhodesia during the touring period.
What aggregate international audience figure do the CNA's institutional pages give for The Family of Man?

Both CNA pages give approximately ten million visitors as the aggregate international audience: the English-language collections page records 'seen by 10 million people throughout the world,' and the educational portal gives 'nearly 10 million visitors.' The conventional secondary 'nine million' figure is unanchored in the in-repo institutional sources -- a contested figure that scholars including Sandeen have flagged for further verification against USIA records.
When did the U.S. government donate the last complete touring version of The Family of Man to Luxembourg?

The CNA chronology dates the donation to the period 1964-1966. The German collections page records that the American government, at Edward Steichen's request, donated to Luxembourg the last complete version of the travelling exhibition.
When was the permanent installation of The Family of Man inaugurated at Clervaux Castle?

Per the CNA's collections chronology, the permanent installation at Clervaux Castle was established in 1994. The exact day and month are not given on either of the CNA collections pages consulted; that finer-grained date is a documented research gap.
What were the dates of the second restoration phase of the Clervaux installation, and who led it?

The second restoration phase ran from September 2010 (closure for renovation) to July 2013 (reopening). The print restoration was led by Studio Berselli, Milan -- with Silvia Berselli, Roberta Piantavigna, Francesca Vantellini, and Isabel Dimas named as the conservators -- while the renovated exhibition rooms were designed by Nathalie Jacoby (NJOY).
What years does the CNA's English collections chronology give for the partial-display period of The Family of Man at Clervaux Castle before the permanent installation?

The CNA's English collections page records the partial-display period as 1974-1989: a selection of the prints was on view at Clervaux Castle, neither the full set nor a permanent canonical installation. The five-year gap between 1989 and the 1994 permanent installation is unaccounted for in the pages consulted.
Which institution today is the custodian of The Family of Man collection at Clervaux Castle?

The Centre national de l'audiovisuel (CNA), Luxembourg's national audiovisual archive, is the institutional custodian of the Clervaux collection. The CNA frames The Family of Man as part of its broader Steichen Collections, alongside Steichen's own photographic archive.
In what year was The Family of Man inscribed on the UNESCO Memory of the World International Register, and which state submitted the nomination?
The Family of Man was inscribed on the UNESCO Memory of the World International Register in 2003. The nomination was submitted in 2002 by Luxembourg.
How many themes does the UNESCO Memory of the World register list for The Family of Man, and how does this compare with the CNA's count?

UNESCO's register page records 'the 32 themes, arranged chronologically.' The CNA Luxembourg educational portal instead describes '37 themes like a photo-essay about human development and cycles of life.' Both are Tier-1-adjacent institutional sources; this is a contested count -- Sandeen and other scholars have argued that the catalog itself does not present a numbered table of sections, so different institutions parse the flow differently. The discrepancy is documented in research/sections.md and is not adjudicated here.
When was the UNESCO Memory of the World programme established?

UNESCO established the Memory of the World Programme in 1992, in response to growing concern about the deterioration and loss of documentary heritage worldwide. The International Register has accepted inscriptions since 1995.
Does inscription on the UNESCO Memory of the World Register confer legal protection on The Family of Man collection?

No. Memory of the World inscription is a form of recognition and visibility, not a legal protection regime. It does not confer ownership rights, does not impose binding conservation standards, and does not create enforceable international law governing the artefact. Legal title to the prints remains with the CNA and the Luxembourg state.
Which 1992-1994 cities does the UNESCO register identify as stops on the pre-inscription tour of restored Family of Man prints?

The UNESCO register page notes that during 1992 and 1993-1994, before the permanent Clervaux installation opened, restored versions traveled internationally including stops in Toulouse, Tokyo, and Hiroshima. The list is explicitly partial ('including stops in').
What is Roland Barthes's central critique of The Family of Man in Mythologies?

Barthes argues that the exhibition's universalising humanism naturalises historical and political difference. In his essay 'The Great Family of Man' (1957), he writes that the show's myth 'rests on a very old mystification, which always consists in placing Nature at the bottom of History.' By grouping photographs under universal categories like birth, death, work, and play, the exhibition represents historically-contingent conditions as eternal human essence. His most-cited challenge: 'Why not ask the parents of Emmet Till, the young Negro assassinated by the Whites, what they think of The Great Family of Man?'
Where did Barthes encounter The Family of Man, and what was its French title?

Barthes encountered The Family of Man at its 1956 Paris stop. The French title used during that showing was La Grande Famille des hommes -- a translation Barthes argues 'amply moralized and sentimentalized' the original meaning of the English phrase, as he argues in his 1957 essay.
What is the title of Eric Sandeen's 1995 book on The Family of Man, and what is its scholarly standing?

Eric Sandeen's book is Picturing an Exhibition: The Family of Man and 1950s America, published by the University of New Mexico Press in 1995. Sandeen argues that the show should be read within the ideological context of 1950s America: Cold War, USIA cultural diplomacy, and mid-century humanism. It is the first book-length scholarly study of the exhibition and the standard Tier-2 anchor for interpretive claims about the exhibition's thematic argument.
What is the central argument of Allan Sekula's 'The Traffic in Photographs' (1981), and how does it apply to The Family of Man?

Sekula argues that photographs carry meanings structured by the institutions that produce and circulate them, rather than by any inherent documentary truth. His Marxist-materialist analysis of mid-century humanist exhibitions -- including The Family of Man -- challenges the universalism that Steichen claimed for the show. Together with Barthes 1957 and Sontag 1977, this essay is one of the three most-cited counter-readings in the critical reception literature on The Family of Man. (The body text of Sekula 1981 has not been fetched in any in-repo session; the institutional-meaning paraphrase here is at the argument-summary level recorded in src-sekula-1981's Relevance section, not at the page level.)
How does Fred Turner read The Family of Man in The Democratic Surround (2013)?

Fred Turner argues that 1940s-50s American liberal thought, drawing on Bauhaus aesthetics and social-scientific theories of personality, produced a new model of democratic communication via immersive multimedia environments. Turner devotes a chapter -- 'The museum of modern art makes the world a family' -- to The Family of Man as a pivotal Cold War cultural event within this liberal-internationalist visual culture. The book is widely cited in recent scholarly discussions of the exhibition's political and aesthetic argument.
How does MoMA's archives-highlights page describe the narrative progression of The Family of Man?

MoMA's archives-highlights page summarises the progression as: an entrance archway with crowd imagery, then lovers, then childbirth, then household life, then careers, then death, then a hydrogen-bomb image, then a return to children and new life, closing on W. Eugene Smith's A Walk to Paradise Garden (1946). This is one institutional parsing -- not a verbatim catalog table of contents.
Who wrote the introduction to the 1955 catalog of The Family of Man, and what framing does it offer?

Edward Steichen wrote the catalog's introduction. In the excerpt MoMA reproduced in its June 21, 1955 press release, Steichen frames the work as 'a mirror of the universal elements and emotions in the everydayness of life -- as a mirror of the essential oneness of mankind throughout the world,' and describes photography as 'a dynamic process of giving form to ideas and of explaining man to man.' This is the curatorial frame that Barthes and Sandeen later contest.
How many plates does Margaret Bourke-White have in The Family of Man, and through which publication is she credited?

Margaret Bourke-White is represented by six plates in The Family of Man. All six are credited 'LIFE, American' in the MoMA Master Checklist, and her plates draw on her Korean War, Czechoslovakia, India, and U.S. assignments.
Where was The Family of Man shown in Paris, and on what evidence does this identification rest?

The Paris stop is conventionally identified as the Musee National d'Art Moderne (then housed at the Palais de Tokyo) in January 1956. The identification is contested at primary level: it is anchored at Tier-3 via the Wikipedia tour-list, supported by institutional-consistency reasoning -- MNAM was at Palais de Tokyo from 1947 until its 1977 move to Centre Pompidou, and the Musee d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris (a different institution) was not founded until 1961, ruling it out. Specific opening and closing dates remain unverified at Tier-1 or Tier-2.
Which photographer's plates in The Family of Man are concentrated in the Childbirth section, and what caption appears beneath one of them?

Wayne Miller's plates #42, #43, and #44 are concentrated in the Childbirth section. Under Caption 4, installed beneath plate #44, appears the Scriabin line 'The universe resounds with the joyful cry I am.' Miller's plates in this section are widely reported in secondary sources as documenting the 1946 birth of his own son, David Miller, though the MoMA Master Checklist itself does not record family provenance.
What was August Sander's life-long photographic project, and when did he establish his studio in Cologne?

August Sander's life-long project was a comprehensive portrait series of the German people entitled "Menschen des 20. Jahrhunderts" (Citizens of the Twentieth Century). Per the ICP archive page, he established his photography studio first in Austria and then in Cologne, where he settled in 1910 and began photographing local peasants, an activity that inspired the project. By the early 1930s he was recognised as an authority on photography in Germany and delivered a series of popular radio lectures, "The Nature and Development of Photography." Political circumstances under National Socialism forced him to discontinue the project, as his son was a Communist Party member (and died in prison in 1944).
What birth name, birthplace, and nationality does the ICP archive record for Brassaï, and what discrepancy exists regarding the publication year of Paris de Nuit?

The ICP archive page records Brassaï's birth name as Gyula Halász, born in the town of Brasov, Transylvania, with dates 1899–1984 and nationality "French (b. Transylvania)." He moved to Paris in 1924 and embraced photography after meeting André Kertész. Regarding Paris de Nuit: the ICP page states it was issued in 1932, while Encyclopædia Britannica and Wikipedia both give 1933. This is a documented discrepancy in the in-repo sources; it is not adjudicated. This date discrepancy is a contested bibliographic point among in-repo sources; neither Britannica nor Wikipedia was re-fetched this session to adjudicate it.
What do the ICP archive page and the MoMA Master Checklist respectively record as Ernst Haas's nationality, and what was his first long color photo essay in LIFE?

The ICP archive page records Ernst Haas as "American," reflecting his post-emigration naturalization; the MoMA Master Checklist records him as "Austrian," reflecting his birth country (Vienna, 1921). Per the ICP page, his "Magic Images of New York" — a twenty-four-page color photo essay — appeared in LIFE in 1951 and is described as both his and LIFE's first long color feature in print. (Note: the Haas Estate biography gives the date as 1953; the discrepancy is recorded but not adjudicated.) Haas joined Magnum in 1949 at Robert Capa's invitation, after his feature "Returning Prisoners of War" appeared in both Heute and LIFE. Both the nationality label and the LIFE essay date are contested across sources; neither discrepancy is adjudicated in the repo.
Who was Andreas Feininger's father, and what was Feininger's educational background per the ICP archive page?

Per the ICP archive page, Andreas Feininger (1906–1999) was born in Paris and was the son of the painter Lyonel Feininger. He was educated in German public schools and at the Weimar Bauhaus, where his interest in photography developed while he was studying architecture. He worked as both architect and photographer in Germany for four years until political circumstances made it impossible, then moved to Paris (where he worked in Le Corbusier's studio) before eventually reaching New York, where he worked for the Black Star Agency and then the U.S. Office of War Information.
What was Ben Shahn's primary profession, and for how long did he work in Roy Stryker's photography department at the Resettlement Administration?

Ben Shahn (1898–1969) was primarily a painter; his initial interest in photography stemmed from its use as a reference tool for his paintings. Per the ICP archive page, he worked in a part-time position in Roy Stryker's photography department at the Resettlement Administration (in Washington DC) from 1935 to 1938 — a three-year period. He used a Leica with a right-angle viewfinder that enabled him to photograph subjects without their knowledge. His single plate in The Family of Man (photo-0377) dates from this FSA period.
What was Gjon Mili's engineering background, and how did he develop his signature photographic technique?

Per the ICP archive page, Gjon Mili (1904–1984) immigrated to the United States in 1923 and studied electrical engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, graduating in 1927. He then worked for Westinghouse as a lighting research engineer until 1938. Through experiments with Harold Edgerton at MIT, he developed tungsten filament lights for color photography; further innovations in stroboscopic and stop-action images brought his work to the attention of LIFE, for which he worked freelance from 1939 until his death. Mili has five plates in The Family of Man (photo-0171, photo-0213, photo-0215, photo-0217, photo-0455).
What was Bill Brandt's association with Man Ray, and what organizations did he photograph for during World War II?

Per the ICP archive page (fetched 2026-05-07), Bill Brandt (1904–1983, born Hamburg) was Man Ray's studio assistant in Paris in 1929, before settling in England in 1931 and working as a freelance documentary photographer for Weekly Illustrated, Picture Post, Lilliput, and other British periodicals. During World War II he photographed air raid shelters for the Ministry of Information and documented endangered buildings for the National Buildings Record. Brandt has four plates in The Family of Man.
Who were the four original staff photographers Henry Luce hired to launch LIFE magazine in 1936, per the ICP archive page for Alfred Eisenstaedt?

Per the ICP archive page for Alfred Eisenstaedt (fetched 2026-05-06), Henry Luce hired Alfred Eisenstaedt, Margaret Bourke-White, Peter Stackpole, and Thomas McAvoy as the four original staff photographers for the new LIFE magazine in 1936. Eisenstaedt, born in Dirschau (now Tczew, Poland) in 1898, had received his first major assignment in 1929 covering the Nobel Prize ceremony in Stockholm.
When did Hiroshi Hamaya join Magnum Photos, and what is the title of his book documenting life in Japan's Snow Country?

Per the ICP archive page (fetched 2026-05-10), Hiroshi Hamaya (1915–1999) became a Magnum member in 1960; the Wikipedia article adds that he was the first Japanese photographer to join Magnum, as an associate member. His book documenting Japan's snow country is Yuki Guni (The Snow Country), published in 1956. Hamaya was born in Tokyo, worked as a freelance photographer since 1937, and received the ICP's Master of Photography Infinity Award in 1986.
What happened to Yosuke Yamahata's photographs during the Tokyo opening of The Family of Man in March 1956, and what press reaction followed?

Steichen and the Japanese executive committee specially added five of Yosuke Yamahata's aftermath photographs from the atomic bombing of Nagasaki to the Tokyo installation. On March 23, 1956 — two days after the opening at Takashimaya Department Store on March 21 — when Emperor Showa visited, one wall was concealed with a white curtain to hide the Nagasaki images. The April 29, 1956 issue of Asahi Graph (The Asahi Picture News) posted a picture of the concealed wall with the headline "Your Highness the Emperor and Prince Yoshi, Please Look at These," so that readers could see what was removed. This controversy is documented in Takenaka 2020 (Popular Inquiry).
On what date and at what venue did The Family of Man open in Tokyo, who promoted it, and how many cities did the Japanese tour visit?

Per Takenaka 2020 (Popular Inquiry, Vol. 1, fetched 2026-05-09), The Family of Man opened in Tokyo on March 21, 1956, at the Takashimaya Department Store. The Japan tour was promoted by MoMA, USIS (United States Information Service), and Nihon Keizai Shimbun (a major financial newspaper). The Japanese executive committee — chaired by Steichen — consisted of photographers Ihee Kimura, Yoshio Watanabe, Shigene Kanemaru, Yasuhiro Ishimoto, graphic designer Takashi Kono, and architect Kenzo Tange (who designed the installation). Per historian Masakazu Inubuse, the Japanese committee reproduced a new set of prints that toured 25 cities, most of them in department stores. The total Japan tour attendance 1956–57 was over one million visitors.
Where and when did The Family of Man appear in South Africa, and what is the context of that showing regarding apartheid legislation?

The CNA educational portal records the South Africa stop as the Government Pavilion, Johannesburg, Union of South Africa, from August 30 to September 13, 1958. At that moment, the Population Registration Act (1950), Group Areas Act (1950), and Separate Amenities Act (1953) were all in full operative force. The Treason Trial against 156 anti-apartheid leaders including Nelson Mandela was ongoing (December 1956 – March 1961). Whether admission to the Government Pavilion was racially segregated or desegregated is an open research question: no source fetched to date addresses it. The USIA agency that commissioned the international tour was simultaneously developing racially calibrated photographic diplomacy targeting African audiences, as documented in Newbury (2024, Penn State UP). Whether the showing was racially integrated or segregated remains an open and contested research question.
What is the central argument of Darren Newbury's 2024 monograph Cold War Photographic Diplomacy, and what archives did it draw on?

Newbury's Cold War Photographic Diplomacy: The US Information Agency and Africa (Penn State UP, 2024) traces the role of photography in the United States' appeal to Africa during the Cold War, concentrating on the period from the mid-1950s through the late 1960s. Drawing on extensive research in USIA archives (NARA RG 306), the book argues that the emergence of newly independent African nations precipitated a contest for influence, leading the US to mount a campaign of photographic diplomacy underpinned by faith in photography's capacity to cross cultural boundaries. The book details how racial integration became a pervasive theme in USIA photographic output — showing racial coexistence in America to visually refute accusations of US racism — while the increasing global visibility of racial injustice undermined those claims.
What new tour-scope figure does the 2025 C2DH dispatch on the Family of Man world tour provide, and what tour stop does it anchor with image evidence?

The 2025 C2DH research dispatch ("Following The Family of Man World Tour" by Emilia Sánchez González, C²DH University of Luxembourg, published March 2025) gives a tour-scope figure of "over 150 cities" — larger than the long-circulating "91 venues" and "120 museums" figures from Wikipedia and other secondary sources. The same article attaches an exhibition poster with the caption "Exhibition poster for The Family of Man in Beirut, Lebanon, 1958," directly anchoring Beirut 1958 as a confirmed tour stop at Tier-2 with image evidence. The article also gives an audience aggregate of "over 9 million visitors" and describes USIS field-post reports in NARA RG 306 as the underlying primary evidence. The "150 cities" figure is contested against older figures (91 venues, 120 museums) derived from Wikipedia and secondary literature; no single NARA primary-archive source has anchored any of these figures definitively.
How many plates does Roy DeCarava have in The Family of Man, and what name spelling variants does the MoMA Master Checklist use for him across those plates?

Roy DeCarava has four plates in The Family of Man (photo-0015 at checklist #18 in the Lovers section, photo-0141 at #147 in Work A, photo-0223 at #232 in Jazz and Blues, and photo-0290 at #301 in Relationships), per strict-match grep against data/photographs.csv. The MoMA Master Checklist uses three different spelling variants across these four plates: "Roy De Carava" (two words, capital D) at #18 and #232; "Roy DeCarava" (one word) at #147; and "Roy de Carava" (two words, lowercase d) at #301. The canonical modern spelling is "Roy DeCarava" — the form the photographer himself used.
What plate numbers and sections account for Wayne Miller's twelve plates in The Family of Man, and which consecutive sequence gives him the highest concentration?

Wayne Miller's twelve plates in The Family of Man are anchored at the plate level by the MoMA Master Checklist. Six appear within the first 47 checklist numbers (#22, #29, #42, #43, #44, #47). Three of those — #42, #43, #44 — are consecutive and form the highest single concentration, all located in the Childbirth section. The plate at #44 carries Caption 4 with the Scriabin line "The universe resounds with the joyful cry I am." Wayne Miller is credited with a LIFE agency affiliation on plate #29 (Mexico) and has plates ranging across Pregnancy, Childbirth, and related sections.
When did John Szarkowski succeed Edward Steichen as Director of the Department of Photography at MoMA?

John Szarkowski was named Director of the Department of Photography at the Museum of Modern Art, effective 1 July 1962, per the MoMA press release (MOMA_1962_0102_99) and confirmed by the Wikipedia article on Szarkowski (fetched 2026-04-30). He was placed in charge of the Edward Steichen Photography Center as well as temporary loan shows of photography. Steichen had served as Director from 1947 to 1962.
What was John Szarkowski's curatorial statement for the 1967 New Documents exhibition, and how does it contrast with Steichen's framing of The Family of Man?

For New Documents (MoMA, February 28 – May 7, 1967), featuring Diane Arbus (32 photographs), Lee Friedlander (30 photographs), and Garry Winogrand (32 photographs), Szarkowski's wall text declared: "In the past decade a new generation of photographers has directed the documentary approach toward more personal ends. Their aim has been not to reform life, but to know it." This is a direct counter to Steichen's framing of The Family of Man as "a mirror of the essential oneness of mankind" — from Steichen's 1955 catalog introduction. Where Steichen mobilised photography for humanist-universalist argument and social reform, Szarkowski valorised personal, anti-rhetorical, anti-redemptive documentary practice.
How many copies of The Family of Man did the USIA circulate internationally, which copy was donated to Luxembourg, and in what year was each of the other copies dispersed?

The USIA circulated four principal copies of The Family of Man internationally. Per the in-repo source entry (src-usia-fom-tour-wind-down, drawing on Wikipedia and CNA sources): Copy 1 (European circulation) was dispersed in 1962; Copy 2 (Central America, India, Africa, Middle East, 1955–1963) was dispersed in 1963; Copy 3 (second European tour, 1957–1965) was donated to Luxembourg in 1965; Copy 4 (South America, Australia, South-East Asia, 1957–1962) was dispersed in 1962. Copy 3 is the collection now permanently installed at Clervaux Castle. Note: this dispersal record is anchored through secondary sources citing USIA records; the NARA RG 306 primary documents were not accessed in any project round to date.
When was the Centre national de l'audiovisuel (CNA) founded, and what institutional relationship does it have with the Family of Man collection?

The CNA (Centre national de l'audiovisuel) was founded in 1989 as Luxembourg's national audiovisual archive. Since the permanent installation of The Family of Man at Clervaux Castle was established in 1994, the CNA has served as the institutional custodian of the collection, framing it as part of the broader Steichen Collections alongside Steichen's own photographic archive. The CNA manages the prints, their conservation, and the public presentation of the exhibition at Clervaux Castle.
Who were the named conservators in the print restoration carried out during the second restoration phase of the Clervaux Family of Man installation?

The second restoration phase at Clervaux (closure September 2010; reopening July 2013) was led by Studio Berselli, Milan. The named conservators were Silvia Berselli, Roberta Piantavigna, Francesca Vantellini, and Isabel Dimas. The renovated exhibition rooms were designed by Nathalie Jacoby (NJOY). These names are recorded in the CNA's English-language collections chronology.
What does the UNESCO nomination form record as the French-language title for The Family of Man, and how does it connect to Barthes's 1957 critique?

The UNESCO nomination for The Family of Man was submitted in 2002 by Luxembourg and inscribed on the Memory of the World International Register in 2003. Both English (2002) and French (2002) nomination forms are in the repository. The French nomination form uses the title "La grande famille des hommes" — the French title Barthes analyzed in his 1957 Mythologies essay as having "amply moralized and sentimentalized" the English phrase "The Family of Man." Barthes argued that the French translation added a moral-redemptive charge absent from the more neutral English.
What specific rhetorical question does Barthes pose in his 1957 Mythologies essay on The Family of Man to challenge the exhibition's universalism?

In "The Great Family of Man" (1957), Barthes poses the question: "Why not ask the parents of Emmet Till, the young Negro assassinated by the Whites, what they think of The Great Family of Man?" This passage is Barthes's sharpest challenge to the exhibition's universalism: the show's myth "rests on a very old mystification, which always consists in placing Nature at the bottom of History." By citing Till — lynched in Mississippi in August 1955, the same year as the MoMA opening — Barthes anchors his abstract critique of naturalised difference in a specific historical atrocity.
What is the exact framing Steichen used in his catalog introduction to describe the aim of The Family of Man?

In the excerpt MoMA reproduced in its June 21, 1955 press release announcing the catalog publication (src-moma-1955-press-release-book), Steichen described The Family of Man as "a mirror of the universal elements and emotions in the everydayness of life -- as a mirror of the essential oneness of mankind throughout the world." He framed photography as "a dynamic process of giving form to ideas and of explaining man to man." This is the primary self-statement of curatorial intent, and it is exactly the passage Barthes and Sandeen later engage as their starting point for critique.
What other USIA-sponsored exhibition toured Japan concurrently with The Family of Man, and what was its attendance?

Per Takenaka (2020, Popular Inquiry), the USIA also sponsored Atoms for Peace / Genshiryoku Heiwariyo Hakurankai, which began touring Japan from November 1, 1955 and visited 10 venues including the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum. Over two and a half million visitors attended the Atoms for Peace exposition over two years. Both shows were USIS-coordinated; their concurrent presence in Japan provides the Cold War cultural-diplomacy context for the Yamahata-photographs controversy at the Family of Man Tokyo opening in March 1956.
What different section-counts for The Family of Man do the UNESCO register and CNA educational portal give, and why might they differ?

UNESCO's register page records "the 32 themes, arranged chronologically," while the CNA Luxembourg educational portal describes "37 themes like a photo-essay about human development and cycles of life." Both are Tier-1-adjacent institutional sources. The discrepancy is documented in research/sections.md and is consistent with the broader scholarly observation (Sandeen 1995 and others) that the catalog itself does not present a numbered table of sections — different institutions have parsed the exhibition's thematic flow differently, counting sub-sections or flow-breaks at different granularities. The project has recorded 41 sections in data/sections.csv as the working list derived from the MoMA Master Checklist, which represents yet another count.
How many distinct scope-aggregate figures exist for The Family of Man world tour in the in-repo sources, and which source gives the largest city-count?

At least seven distinct figures appear across in-repo sources: 91 venues / 37 countries (Wikipedia derivative, Turner 2012); 9M / 61 countries / 91 venues (O'Brian 2008); 9M / 69 countries / 6 USIA copies (Córdova 2013); 10M / 10 copies (CNA Luxembourg education); 91 venues / 38 countries (Polish Wikipedia); 120 museums (Cuartoscuro 2014); 150+ cities / 9M / 250 photographers (C²DH 2025 dispatch by Sánchez González). The largest city-count figure ("over 150 cities") comes from the 2025 C²DH research dispatch, drawn from the FoMLEG project's ongoing NARA archival research. No single primary archival source has yet anchored any of these figures to a NARA RG 306 master tour log.
What is Edward Steichen's birth name, birth date, and approximate age when his family emigrated from Luxembourg to the United States?

Edward Steichen's birth name was Edouard Jean Steichen. He was born on 27 March 1879 in Bivange, Luxembourg. Per the CNA's biographical page, he was barely two years old when his parents emigrated to the United States. He later anglicized his first name from Edouard to Edward. He died in 1973 in West Redding, Connecticut.
What is the MoMA exhibition record number for The Family of Man, and how is it used in this project?

The Family of Man is MoMA Exhibition #569. Its MoMA exhibition history record is indexed as "Exh. #569" (or "Exhibition 2429" in the MoMA online calendar, per src-moma-exhibition-record-2429 in the repository). The source id "src-moma-exh-0569-master-checklist" refers to the MoMA Exh. #569 Master Checklist — the project's most-cited Tier-1 source for plate-level attribution data.
What is the publisher and year of Sandeen 1995, and what is its primary interpretive claim about The Family of Man?

Eric Sandeen's Picturing an Exhibition: The Family of Man and 1950s America was published by the University of New Mexico Press in 1995. It is the first book-length scholarly study of the exhibition. Sandeen argues that the show should be read within the ideological context of 1950s America — specifically the Cold War, USIA cultural diplomacy, and mid-century humanism — rather than as an unmediated humanist statement. His most important chapter, "The family of man on the move," addresses the USIA-commissioned international tour and its ideological function. The book is the standard Tier-2 anchor for interpretive claims about the exhibition's thematic argument.
Where did the separate international edition of The Family of Man open in the United States, and on what dates?

Per the June 21, 1955 MoMA press release, a separate international edition of The Family of Man opened at the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., from June 30 to July 31, 1955. This was distinct from the main domestic tour, which was slated for six U.S. cities (Minneapolis, Dallas, Cleveland, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Pittsburgh). The Washington Corcoran showing was the first stop for the USIA's international touring version.
How many works by Japanese photographers were specially added to the Tokyo installation of The Family of Man, and which photographer's atomic-bomb images were included?

Per Takenaka 2020 (Popular Inquiry, p. 47, fetched 2026-05-09), Steichen and the Japanese executive committee decided to add 60 works by Japanese photographers to make the Tokyo installation special. Among those additions were five photographs by Yosuke Yamahata documenting the aftermath of the atomic bombing of Nagasaki. It was these Yamahata images that were concealed behind a white curtain when Emperor Showa visited on March 23, 1956, triggering the press controversy.
What is the institutional significance of The Family of Man's 2003 UNESCO Memory of the World inscription for the Clervaux collection?

The 2003 UNESCO Memory of the World inscription recognizes the Clervaux collection as a document of international significance — but not as a legal protection regime. Per the UNESCO IAC programme page (src-unesco-mow-iac-programme-about, in repo), Memory of the World inscription does not confer legal ownership rights, does not impose binding conservation standards, and does not create enforceable international law. Legal title to the prints remains with the CNA and the Luxembourg state. The inscription functions as enhanced visibility and recognition, supporting the CNA's international exhibition-loan and conservation activities.
What was David "Chim" Seymour's birth name and nationality, per Encyclopædia Britannica, and how many plates does he have in The Family of Man?

Per the Encyclopædia Britannica entry for David Seymour (src-britannica-david-seymour, in repo), his birth name was Dawid Szymin, born November 20, 1911 in Warsaw, Poland. He was a co-founder of Magnum Photos in 1947 alongside Henri Cartier-Bresson, Robert Capa, George Rodger, and William Vandivert. David Seymour has four plates in The Family of Man per the Magnum photographer bios and MoMA Master Checklist. He was killed by machine-gun fire near the Suez Canal on November 11, 1956, just under two years after The Family of Man opened.
In what year did Steichen receive his MoMA appointment as Director of Photography, and what year did he retire?

Per the CNA Luxembourg educational portal (src-cna-edu-steichen-bio, Tier 1), Edward Steichen served as Director of the Department of Photography at the Museum of Modern Art from 1947 to 1962. He was born in 1879 and had already been active in photography for over four decades before his MoMA appointment. His successor John Szarkowski was named Director effective July 1, 1962.
Why does the MoMA Master Checklist record Robert Frank's nationality as "Swiss" rather than American, and how many plates does he have?

The MoMA Master Checklist credits all seven of Robert Frank's plates as "Swiss" because Frank had not yet naturalized as a U.S. citizen at the time of the 1955 opening. He was born in Zurich in 1924 and emigrated to the United States in 1947, but his naturalization postdated the exhibition. His seven plates span photographs taken in the USA, Spain, Peru, Wales, and England, drawn from his early-1950s freelance period. The ICP archive page for Frank (src-icp-frank-archive) records his dates as 1924–2019 (Frank died September 9, 2019) and nationality as "American (b. Switzerland)."
Did Edward Steichen ever visit the Family of Man collection in Luxembourg, and at what age?

Yes. The in-repo source entry (src-steichen-1966-luxembourg-visit, in the 1960s sources folder) documents Steichen's 1966 visit to Luxembourg in connection with the donated collection. He was 87 years old at the time of the visit (born March 27, 1879; visiting in 1966). This visit occurred the year after the USIA donation of Copy 3 to Luxembourg (1965). Steichen died in 1973.
